extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners performing SME analyses)
extracted.subtask_description: A worksheet to analyze a patent claim for subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 (focus on abstract ideas) following the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance; intended to be used per-claim to guide Steps 1, 2A, and 2B of the eligibility flowchart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify what applicant invented
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention. (MPEP 2103(I))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the disclosure to state what the applicant invented in Section I. A separate worksheet should be used to analyze each claim. This step grounds later comparisons between the claim and any identified abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construe the claim in accordance with BRI before performing the eligibility analysis; record the BRI in Section I so subsequent determinations (e.g., whether the claim recites an abstract idea) reflect that interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category check (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the claimed invention fall within one of the four statutory categories of invention (process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose A or B: A) If yes, identify which statutory category and continue SME analysis. B) If no, make a rejection of the claim as being drawn to non-statutory subject matter (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01). If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, it is recommended to continue the SME analysis under that assumption and make the assumption clear in the record; consider suggesting a potential amendment to applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is 'directed' to an abstract idea when the abstract idea is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim. Courts have found concepts such as fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves (standing alone), or mathematical relationships/formulae to be abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose A, B, or C: A) No — claim does not recite a concept similar to those found abstract; conclude SME and continue with other patentability requirements. B) Yes but streamlined analysis appropriate — eligibility is self-evident and a full analysis not needed. C) Yes — identify the limitation(s) that recite the abstract idea and explain why those limitations are an abstract idea; then continue with Step 2B. Assistance: refer to case law chart and 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use streamlined analysis if eligibility is self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: Yes, but the streamlined analysis is appropriate as the eligibility is self-evident, and a full eligibility analysis is not needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply streamlined analysis when applicant's claimed invention, as explained in Section I, is not focused on the abstract idea and the claim clearly does not attempt to tie up an abstract idea such that others cannot practice it. Refer to February 2015 Training Slides for examples of when streamlined analysis is appropriate. Conclude SME analysis and proceed with other patentability considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify claim limitation(s) that recite the abstract idea and explain why
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to an abstract idea, identify the limitation(s) in the claim that set forth or describe the abstract idea and explain why the recited subject matter is an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List the specific claim elements that recite the abstract idea and provide reasons why those limitations are considered abstract (e.g., they recite a fundamental economic practice, a method of organizing human activity, an idea standing alone, or a mathematical relationship/formula). Continue to Step 2B after identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of additional elements beyond the abstract idea (Step 2B - threshold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there any additional elements (features/limitations/step) recited in the claim beyond the abstract idea identified above?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose 1 or 2: 1) No — if there are no other elements, conclude SME analysis by making a §101 rejection (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015). Consider whether disclosure contains elements that could be added to render the claim eligible and identify them for possible suggestions to applicant. 2) Yes — list the claim elements in addition to the abstract idea and continue with evaluation of their significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate significance of additional elements — search for an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying additional elements and evaluating their significance involves the search for an 'inventive concept' in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all identified additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea. Reasons supporting significance can include one or more of the following: improves another technology or technical field; improves the functioning of a computer itself; applies the abstract idea with, or by use of, a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic functions; not adding the words 'apply it'); effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adds a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field (not appending well-understood, routine, and conventional activities at a high level of generality); adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (not insignificant extrasolution activity such as mere data gathering); adds meaningful limitations that amount to more than generally linking the use of the abstract idea to a particular technological environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude whether the claim amounts to 'significantly more' (Step 2B conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the additional elements, individually or in combination, result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If yes, state why the additional elements amount to significantly more and conclude SME analysis (then continue with other patentability requirements). If no, conclude SME analysis by making a §101 rejection and continue with other patentability requirements (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015). If appropriate, clarify the record with remarks explaining how the claim both recites an abstract idea and nevertheless amounts to significantly more due to particular elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest amendments and record assumptions when applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category or include elements that might make it eligible, identify and consider suggesting those elements to applicant; make any assumptions clear in the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no amendment is possible, conclude SME analysis and continue examination under other patentability requirements. If analyzing under an assumption (e.g., claim amended to a statutory category), explicitly record that assumption in the Office action. Identify elements from the disclosure that might be added to the claim to achieve eligibility and propose them to applicant where appropriate.
